work_order.confidence_rationale: Reproduced independently of the previous run: in Chromium against the live app at $PREVIEW_URL following the reporter's exact steps, and again in the repo's own vitest harness driving the real sql.js REGEXP user function. The throwing line was read in both platform files and the two sibling guards were read. Both objections from the last review were checked rather than assumed, and both are upheld: `#\d+` provably matches zero demo notes (returns rows=0 against a table that contains a `#mortgage` note), and the `#mortgage` row count is produced by a date-gated loop plus an RNG, so it is not a safe constant. The fix itself is unverified, which is the implementer's job. I could not run Firefox (only Chromium is installed here), but the throwing code is platform-independent JavaScript on the shared web/sql.js path, and it reproduces in vitest, so no Firefox-specific behaviour is plausible.
work_order.understanding: Typing a backslash into the value of a `notes matches` rule condition crashes the app with the red 'Something internally went wrong' banner. The trigger is not the final value but the intermediate keystrokes on the way to it. RuleEditor re-runs its live preview on every keystroke (packages/desktop-client/src/components/rules/RuleEditor.tsx:1086-1105): `send('make-filters-from-conditions')` turns the condition into `{ notes: { $regexp: value } }`, the AQL compiler inlines the user-supplied pattern as the SQL literal `REGEXP('<value>', <field>)`, and the SQLite user function `regexp` does an unguarded `new RegExp(regex)`. After typing `#` then a backslash, the intermediate value `#\` is an incomplete regex and `new RegExp` throws a SyntaxError from inside the SQL engine, so it escapes every application-level caller: it rejects the `aqlQuery` promise in RuleEditor's `run()` (called as `void run()` with no `.catch()`), and the backend separately emits `server-error`, which `handleGlobalEvents` turns into the banner. I reproduced the full matrix live on the demo budget, one keystroke at a time: `#mortgage` typed through all 9 characters produced no banner and no page errors at any step, while a single `\` and the sequence `#`,`\` both produced the banner plus 2 errors, the console showing `[Exception] Error at c.handleError ... at runQuery$1 ... at runQuery`. The `#\d+` case is the sharpest evidence, because its final value is a perfectly valid regex and yet it still crashes: the banner appears at the second keystroke (`#\`), proving the throw happens per-keystroke rather than on the final value.
work_order.root_cause: The SQLite `REGEXP` user function calls `new RegExp(regex)` with no try/catch, so any syntactically incomplete pattern the user happens to have typed mid-edit throws a SyntaxError from inside the SQL engine rather than returning a value. Because the throw bypasses application error handling it both rejects the caller's promise (unhandled in RuleEditor's `void run()`) and triggers the global `server-error` banner. A partial regex is a normal transient state while typing, not an exceptional one, so the data layer must treat an unparseable pattern as 'matches nothing' -- which is exactly what the two sibling regex consumers already do (`Condition.eval` at packages/loot-core/src/server/rules/condition.ts:421-427 and `evaluateClause` at packages/loot-core/src/server/forecast/forecast-filters.ts:254-259). The sqlite `regexp` function is the one consumer that was missed.
work_order.approach: Wrap the `new RegExp` call in the sqlite `REGEXP` user function in a try/catch that returns 0 (no match), matching the existing precedent in `Condition.eval` and `evaluateClause`. This is the correct fix location rather than a guard in RuleEditor: `regexp` is the single chokepoint every `$regexp` query reaches, so one guard there fixes the rule-editor preview and every sibling caller at once. Two independent `$regexp` producers feed it -- `conditionsToAQL`'s `matches` case (packages/loot-core/src/server/transactions/transaction-rules.ts:652-653), which backs both the rule editor and the `FilterButton` used by custom reports and the accounts header (packages/desktop-client/src/components/filters/FiltersMenu.tsx emits `RuleConditionEntity`), and the `hasTags`/`hasAnyTag` cases at lines 685 and 701 -- whereas patching RuleEditor would leave all of them still crashing. Apply the identical change to both platform registrations (`platform/server/sqlite/index.ts` for the browser/sql.js build and `index.electron.ts` for better-sqlite3), since they define the function separately. Do not change AQL compilation or the rule editor: an invalid pattern should still compile and simply match nothing, so a saved rule with an in-progress regex stays inert rather than breaking.

Registration at line 259 (`db.create_function('REGEXP', regexp)`) is unchanged.

Assert that no 'Something internally went wrong' notification appears at ANY point, that the condition editor remains rendered and interactive, and that the browser console records no unhandled rejection. On the current code the banner appears at the second keystroke (`#\`). Note that the completed value `#\d+` is only the end of the input sequence, not evidence of anything by itself -- it is a valid regex that matches no demo note, so seeing an empty preview for it is correct behaviour and is asserted separately in AC-3.

acceptance.check: POSITIVE CONTROL: a valid regex that does match demo data still matches after the fix. Do not assert an exact row count; the count is produced by a date-gated generator loop and is not a stable constant.

If the welcome tour modal appears, click 'Take the tour' then 'Skip tour' to dismiss it; it overlays the Rules page and will otherwise intercept clicks.
In the first condition row set the field to `notes` and the operator to `matches`.

POSITIVE CONTROL: type `#mortgage` into the value input and wait ~2s. Assert the 'This rule applies to these transactions' table is NOT empty and contains at least one Housy House / Mortgage row. Do NOT assert an exact row count -- the count varies with the day of month the demo is generated. This control is mandatory: without it, every 'no banner' assertion below would also pass against a guard that returns no-match for every pattern.
Clear the input. Type `#`, then a single backslash, then `d`, then `+` -- one keystroke at a time, pausing ~1s between characters so each intermediate value is previewed.

Assert no red 'Something internally went wrong' notification appears at ANY point, that the condition editor is still rendered and interactive, and that the console shows no unhandled rejection. On the current code the banner appears at the `#\` keystroke.
Clear the input and type just a single backslash; assert again that no error banner appears and the preview table is simply empty.
Clear the input and type `asdfasdf\`; assert again that no error banner appears.

Clear the input and type `#\d+` -- also a VALID regex, which matches nothing because no demo note contains a digit after the '#'. Confirm there is no banner and the preview is empty. (The crash on this input happens at the intermediate `#\` keystroke in step 8, not at the completed value.)

evidence: Browser, $PREVIEW_URL (chromium, demo budget), following the reporter's exact steps (Rules > Create new rule, field `notes`, op `matches`), typing one keystroke at a time with ~1.1s between characters. Result matrix: `#mortgage` typed through all 9 characters -> no banner and 0 page errors at every step, preview populated (Housy House / Mortgage rows and Deposit rows visible); `\` -> banner shown, 2 errors; `#`,`\`,`d`,`+` -> banner appears at the second keystroke (`#\`), 2 errors. This reproduces the report and shows the trigger is the backslash, not the field/operator selection. After the crash the input value itself resets to a single character, confirming the component was torn down and remounted by the error.

The console stack for the failing cases confirms the throw escapes the SQL engine into the query path: `[Exception] Error at c.handleError ... at a.step ... at runQuery$1 ... at runQuery ... at execQuery$1 ... at execTransactionsBasic ... at runCompiledAqlQuery ... at compileAndRunAqlQuery`.

Reproduced a third time in the repo's own vitest harness against the real sql.js REGEXP user function, seeded with a row whose note is `#mortgage note`. Exact output: `n.` => OK rows=1; `#mortgage` => OK rows=1; `normal` => OK rows=0; `#\d+` => OK rows=0; `\` => THREW; `asdfasdf\` => THREW; `#\` => THREW; `#[` => THREW; `(` => THREW. This isolates the failure to the sqlite function itself, independent of the UI. Command: `yarn workspace @actual-app/core exec vitest run src/platform/server/sqlite/regexp-repro.test.ts` (scratch file, since removed).

OBJECTION 1 UPHELD, and it invalidates the previous plan's AC-2 as written. The same vitest matrix shows `#\d+` is a well-formed regex that returns 0 rows against a table that DOES contain a `#mortgage` note -- it does not throw and it does not match. Statically confirmed too: every `#[0-9]` occurrence in packages/loot-core/src/mocks/budget.ts is a hex colour in the tag-definition table (lines 28, 36, 41, 46, 54, 60, 63, 65, 66, 69), never note text, and the full tag vocabulary built by getTagNotes (lines 80-121) contains no digit. So no demo note matches `#\d+`. The previous AC-2 asserted that `#\d+` 'shows the transactions whose notes match' while its own how_to_verify pivoted to a different pattern (`#mortgage`) with the opposite expected outcome -- a rule and a worked example that contradict each other, and as a control it could not distinguish 'valid regex still matches' from 'the guard returns no-match for everything'. AC-2 has been rewritten around `#mortgage` with a non-empty assertion, and the `#\d+` behaviour is now stated correctly on its own in AC-3.

OBJECTION 2 UPHELD as a safety claim, though the number happens to have been reproducible today. I measured the `#mortgage` preview at exactly 10 rendered rows with 2 Housy House rows across three fresh playwright-UA sessions and one fresh non-playwright (Firefox) UA session -- so 10 is not simply wrong. But it is not a safe constant to assert: the demo's `#mortgage` rows come partly from a bills loop gated on `isBefore(date, currentDay)` (packages/loot-core/src/mocks/budget.ts:317-353), so the count depends on the day of month the budget is generated, and partly from `pickRandom` over the expense payee list for the account-transaction fill, which is unseeded `Math.random` outside playwright (packages/loot-core/src/mocks/random.ts exports `Platform.isPlaywright ? pseudoRandom : Math.random`). Today is the 2nd of the month, which is close to the worst case for the gate. Every exact count has therefore been removed from the plan in favour of a non-empty assertion plus a named Housy House / Mortgage row.

Confirmed the throwing line in both platform files, which define `regexp` independently: packages/loot-core/src/platform/server/sqlite/index.ts:211-213 (registered at line 259 via `db.create_function('REGEXP', regexp)`) and packages/loot-core/src/platform/server/sqlite/index.electron.ts:124-126 (registered at line 139 via `db.function('REGEXP', { deterministic: true }, regexp)`). Both are a bare `new RegExp(regex).test(text || '')` with no guard.

Confirmed the two sibling regex consumers already guard and return no-match: `Condition.eval` wraps `new RegExp` in try/catch at packages/loot-core/src/server/rules/condition.ts:421-427 (`logger.log('invalid regexp in matches condition', e); return false;`) and `evaluateClause` does the same for `$regexp` at packages/loot-core/src/server/forecast/forecast-filters.ts:254-259. The sqlite `regexp` function is the one consumer that was missed.

Confirmed the fix location is the shared chokepoint rather than the UI: `conditionsToAQL`'s `matches` case at packages/loot-core/src/server/transactions/transaction-rules.ts:652-653 emits `$regexp`, and the `hasTags`/`hasAnyTag` cases at lines 685 and 701 emit `$regexp` too; the AQL compiler turns every `$regexp` into `REGEXP(...)` at packages/loot-core/src/server/aql/compiler.ts:737-740. `FilterButton` in packages/desktop-client/src/components/filters/FiltersMenu.tsx offers `matches` and emits `RuleConditionEntity` to custom reports and the accounts header, so those callers reach the same unguarded function -- a RuleEditor-only guard would leave them crashing.

Confirmed the crash surface, not just the crash: the rejected `aqlQuery` promise in RuleEditor is called as `void run()` with no `.catch()` (packages/desktop-client/src/components/rules/RuleEditor.tsx:1104), so it becomes an unhandled page rejection; independently the backend emits `server-error` and `handleGlobalEvents` (packages/desktop-client/src/global-events.ts:23-25) dispatches `addGenericErrorNotification`, producing the banner.

Scope note on coverage: the reproduction exercised the web/sql.js build in Chromium. Only Chromium is installed on this runner, so the reporter's Firefox was not tested directly. The crashing code is platform-independent JavaScript evaluated inside SQLite, and it reproduces identically in the vitest harness, so no Firefox-specific behaviour is plausible -- but the fix must be applied to the better-sqlite3 (Electron) registration as well, which is asserted by the test and by the two-file change list rather than by a browser run.

Confirmed the demo budget is NOT an empty template (a premise the earlier review wrongly challenged). `default-db.sqlite` really does contain 0 accounts and 0 transactions, but `createDemoBudget` calls `createTestBudget` at packages/loot-core/src/server/budgetfiles/app.ts:463 after copying that file, and `createTestBudget` (packages/loot-core/src/mocks/budget.ts:746) creates 8 accounts and a full transaction set whose notes carry tags like `#mortgage`, `#utilities` and `#groceries`. Confirmed live: the Rules sidebar lists 8 accounts and the `#mortgage` preview returns rows. No `#123` fixture is needed and none exists.

alternatives_considered.approach: Add a try/catch around the `aqlQuery` call in RuleEditor's preview effect, so a bad pattern just yields an empty preview list.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Fixes the symptom at one call site and leaves the crash live for every other `$regexp` consumer -- the `matches` filter in custom reports and the accounts header goes through the same `conditionsToAQL` -> `$regexp` -> `REGEXP()` path. One guard in the shared sqlite function is both the smaller diff and the correct fix.

alternatives_considered.approach: Validate the regex in `Condition`'s parse step (or in `conditionsToAQL`) and reject the condition with an 'Invalid regex' field error, mirroring the existing `assert` error types.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Plausible as a UX improvement, but it changes user-visible behaviour well beyond the reported bug (a previously accepted rule with an invalid pattern would start erroring) and it does not protect the other `$regexp` callers. Worth a follow-up ticket, not this fix.

alternatives_considered.approach: Escape or otherwise normalise the pattern in the AQL compiler's `$regexp` case before inlining it as a SQL string literal.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Addresses a real adjacent weakness (the compiler only escapes single quotes) but it is not the cause here. The value reaching SQLite is correct -- `#\d+` is the user's intended regex, and the vitest matrix shows it is well-formed and simply matches nothing -- and the throw happens in the JS engine after the SQL string is well-formed. Escaping would change matching semantics for every valid regex.

alternatives_considered.approach: Escape the backslash before compiling so `#\` is treated as a literal backslash rather than an incomplete escape.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Wrong semantics. `matches` is a documented regex operator; users type `\d`, `\s`, `\\` deliberately. Escaping would break every working regex to fix the crash.

alternatives_considered.approach: Debounce the live preview so intermediate keystrokes are never queried.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Would reduce how often the crash fires but not remove it -- paste, autofill, and any single invalid keystroke still throws. It hides the throw rather than fixing the cause.

risks: Returning 0 for an invalid pattern means such a query silently matches nothing. That matches the behaviour already established for `Condition.eval` and `forecast-filters`, so a rule saved with a broken pattern is inert rather than destructive -- but a typo in a regex is quiet. A follow-up UX ticket for a visible 'invalid regex' field error would address that.

The fix touches a shared SQLite function used by every `$regexp` query. The guard is additive and only changes behaviour on the previously-throwing path, so valid patterns are unaffected -- but `yarn test` should be run in full to confirm nothing depended on the throw.

`regexp` is registered separately in the sql.js and better-sqlite3 platform files. Missing the Electron one would leave the desktop build crashing on the same input, so both files must change in the same commit.

This addresses the crash only. The unhandled `void run()` rejection in RuleEditor's preview effect remains a latent way for any future query error to surface as a full-app error banner; that is a separate robustness concern, not part of this fix.
out_of_scope: Showing a visible 'Invalid regex' error on the rule condition field instead of a silently empty preview -- a UX follow-up, deliberately not bundled with the crash fix.
Adding a `.catch()` to RuleEditor's `void run()` preview effect to stop any query failure from becoming a global error banner. Related but a distinct robustness change with its own trade-offs.

Making the demo budget's transaction generation deterministic, which is what would be needed to assert an exact `#mortgage` row count. Out of scope here; the acceptance criteria avoid depending on a count instead.
The upstream issue at actualbudget/actual#6317 remains open; this fixes the crash in this copy only.

review.title: The new `logger.log('invalid regexp in sqlite REGEXP', e)` sits inside the per-row user function, so it fires once for EVERY row SQLite scans, not once per query. RuleEditor re-runs the preview query on every keystroke (RuleEditor.tsx:1084-1106, `useEffect` on `conditions`), so typing one character of a partial regex against a real budget produces one console.log of a full SyntaxError stack per transaction, per keystroke. `verboseMode` defaults to `true` (platform/server/log/index.ts:3) and nothing in the desktop-client or desktop-electron trees calls `setVerboseMode(false)` -- the only caller is server/main.ts:304, which is the node server path, not the Electron or browser build.

`packages/loot-core/src/platform/server/sqlite/index.ts:219`

Evidence: Measured in the repo's own vitest harness against the real sql.js REGEXP function (scratch test, reverted). With console.log stubbed to a counter, a single query over 5000 seeded rows with an unparseable pattern produced exactly 5000 console.log calls (123ms, vs 18ms and 0 calls for a valid pattern). With logging live, a query over 10000 rows took 1122ms versus 30ms for the same query with a valid pattern; with logging stubbed the same 10000-row invalid query took 237ms, so roughly 4/5 of the cost is the logging, not the throw/catch. Scaled to plausible budget sizes with logging live: 1000 rows = 186ms, 3000 rows = 356ms, 10000 rows = 1122ms -- superlinear, because each logged SyntaxError carries a stack trace. The rule editor's preview selects from `transactions` unindexed, so every keystroke pays the full table scan.

Fix: Do not log per row. Either hoist the failure out of the hot path (compile the pattern once per query, or memoize a set of known-invalid patterns and log only the first time a given pattern is seen), or drop the log entirely and rely on the silent no-match, which is what `evaluateClause` in forecast-filters.ts:257-259 already does -- note it uses a bare `catch {}` with no logging at all. If a log is wanted, keep it but rate-limit it to once per distinct pattern string.

review.title: The PR replaces a throw-on-first-row with a scan of every row that logs a full SyntaxError (message plus stack) once per row. That is a new cost on the exact hot path the rule editor drives on every keystroke, and the PR's own cited precedent for the guard does not log at all. `evaluateClause` (forecast-filters.ts:254-259) uses a bare `catch { return false; }`; `Condition.eval` (condition.ts:421-427) does log, but it runs once per transaction inside the JS rule engine, not once per row of an unindexed SQL scan driven by a text input.

`packages/loot-core/src/platform/server/sqlite/index.ts:219`

Evidence: Reproduced in the repo's own vitest harness against the real sql.js/better-sqlite3 REGEXP user function (scratch test, reverted). With `console.log` replaced by a counter, one query with an unparseable pattern over 5000 seeded rows produced exactly 5000 log calls -- 1:1 with rows scanned, so the count grows with the budget. Timed with `process.hrtime.bigint()` on the node/better-sqlite3 path: 10000 rows took 629.8ms with real `console.log`, 63.9ms with the log stubbed, and 8.7ms for the same query with a valid pattern -- roughly 90% of the wall-clock is the logging, and it is ~70x the cost of a matching query. Pre-fix the same query threw on row 1 and returned immediately, so this is a cost the PR introduces, not one it inherits. `verboseMode` defaults to `true` (platform/server/log/index.ts:1) and the only `setVerboseMode` call in the repo is server/main.ts:304, gated on `config.verbose !== undefined`; nothing in desktop-client, desktop-electron or packages/api passes it, so `logger.log` reaches the console on every build the reporter could have used.

Fix: Drop the `logger.log` and use a bare `catch { return 0; }`, matching `evaluateClause`. If a log is wanted for debuggability, include the pattern string and emit it at most once per distinct pattern (a module-level `Set` of already-logged patterns is enough) -- but the silent no-match is what the two sibling consumers already do, so the smaller diff is the right one.

review.title: The first assertion of the new test, `REGEXP('\\', string)`, is a no-op: it returns `[]` on the UNFIXED code too, because SQLite does not process backslash escapes in string literals, so the regex the function actually receives is the two-character string `\\` (an escaped backslash) -- which is a perfectly valid regex matching no row. Only the `#[` and `(` assertions in that test actually fail before the fix. The test as a whole is still a valid regression test (it fails pre-fix, verified), so this is about the assertion not testing what its comment claims, not about the test being useless.

Evidence: Ran each of the PR's exact SQL literals against the UNFIXED index.ts (fix reverted, tests kept): `REGEXP('\\', string)` => `[]` (no throw); `REGEXP('#[', string)` => THREW; `REGEXP('(', string)` => THREW; `REGEXP('#mortgage', string)` => `[{"id":"id1"}]`; `REGEXP('normal', string)` => `[]`; `REGEXP('#\\d+', string)` => `[]`. Separately probed what SQLite hands the function: `SELECT ('\\')` returns the 2-char string `\\`, and `SELECT ('#\\d+')` returns `#\\d+` -- confirming no backslash unescaping occurs. The same substitution affects the third new test: its `#\\d+` case is really the regex `#\\d+` (literal-backslash followed by `d+`), not the `#\d+` the work order's AC-3 describes, so it does not exercise the digit-matching pattern either. The regression the work order's evidence documents -- `\`, `#\` throwing -- is only covered by the transaction-rules.test.ts cases, not by the sqlite-level assertions.

Fix: Write the literals the way the compiler actually produces them, not double-escaped for JS. The AQL compiler inlines the raw user string into a single-quoted SQL literal with only `'` -> `''` escaping (compiler.ts:355-357), so a one-character backslash reaches SQLite as `'\'` -- one backslash in the SQL source. In a JS double-quoted string that is `"REGEXP('\\', string)"`. The transaction-rules.test.ts cases (`'\\'`, `'#\\'`) are already correct and cover it; the sqlite-level duplicates should either be corrected the same way or dropped as redundant.

review.title: The loop `for (const value of ['\\', '#\\', '#[', '(', 'asdfasdf\\'])` asserts only that the query resolves to `[]`. It does not distinguish 'the guard returned no-match' from 'the query silently matched nothing for some unrelated reason' -- e.g. a wrong field name or a broken filter would produce the same `[]` and pass. The sibling sqlite-level test does check the positive direction, so the suite as a whole is sound; this is about the loop alone being one-sided.

Evidence: The loop's `expect(transactions).toEqual([])` would pass for any of: field name typo'd, `$regexp` never emitted, or the guard returning 0 unconditionally (the exact failure mode AC-2 exists to rule out). The test does have a positive assertion immediately after the loop (`'#mortgage'` -> `['1']`), which is what makes the negative results meaningful -- but only for the single `'#mortgage'` case, not per-value.

review.title: The second new test, `should not throw on an unparseable regex when no rows are scanned`, cannot fail: with no rows scanned SQLite never invokes the user function, and the pattern it uses (`REGEXP('\\'`) is itself a valid regex once SQLite's no-backslash-unescaping is accounted for. It passes identically before and after the fix and asserts nothing about the guard. Evidence: Ran both new sqlite tests against the UNFIXED `index.ts` (fix reverted in place, tests kept): `should not throw on an unparseable regex, matching nothing instead` FAILS (SyntaxError on `#[`), while `should not throw on an unparseable regex when no rows are scanned` PASSES. Also probed what the function actually receives: `SELECT ('\\')` yields the 2-character string `\\` (`length` = 2), confirming SQLite passes backslashes through untouched, so the pattern is an escaped backslash -- a valid regex that matches nothing.

review.title: A missed second crash path of the same family as the one being fixed, reachable from the same rule editor. The Handlebars `regex`/`replace`/`replaceAll` helpers call `new RegExp` unguarded, and -- contrary to the correctness review's assessment -- the save-time check in `Action`'s constructor does NOT validate them when the template's first argument is a field reference, because the constructor renders with an empty context and the helper short-circuits on `value == null` before ever compiling the pattern. The apply-time call is unwrapped, so the SyntaxError escapes rule application entirely. Pre-existing and out of this PR's declared scope; a follow-up ticket, not a reason to hold this PR.

`packages/loot-core/src/server/rules/handlebars-helpers.ts:52`

Evidence: Ran against `Action` directly (scratch test, reverted). `new Action('set', 'notes', null, { template: '{{regex notes "#[" ""}}' })` constructs WITHOUT throwing -- `Action` renders the template with `{}` at action.ts:63-66, so `notes` is `undefined` and `regexHelper` returns `null` at its `if (value == null) return null` guard (handlebars-helpers.ts:32-34) without reaching `new RegExp`. The same construct with a literal first argument, `{{regex "hello" "#[" ""}}`, DOES throw `Invalid Handlebars template` at construction -- which is exactly why the existing guard looks sufficient when tested with literals. At apply time `a.exec({ notes: 'hello' })` THREW `Invalid regular expression: /#[/: Unterminated character class`, and `{{regex notes "/#[/g" ""}}` throws the same way. Propagation is unguarded: `exec`'s Handlebars branch (action.ts:150-152) has no try/catch, unlike the formula branch immediately above it which catches and pushes to `_ruleErrors`; `execNonSplitActions` (rule.ts:15-19) is a bare `actions.forEach(action => action.exec(update))`; and `runRules` calls `rules[i].execActions(finalTrans)` (transaction-rules.ts:390) with no handler, from `accounts/sync.ts:838`. Reachability from the UI: the action template is a free-text input (RuleEditor.tsx:550), and `isTemplatingEnabled = actionTemplating || templated` (RuleEditor.tsx:506) keeps templating editable once a template exists, so the `actionTemplating` flag defaulting off does not close this.

Fix: Out of scope for PR #11 -- do not expand this diff. File a follow-up ticket. The fix there is the same three lines applied here: wrap the `new RegExp` calls in `regexHelper` in a try/catch returning the input unchanged, or wrap the apply-time `handlebarsTemplate` call in `Action.exec` in the same try/catch the formula branch already has.

failure_packet.raw_excerpt:
sdlc: the agent did not write qa-report.json.
It reported success, so it ran — it just put the file somewhere else, or never wrote one.
JSON files that do exist: .nano-staged.json, .oxfmtrc.json, .oxlintrc.json, knip.json, package.json, tsconfig.json, tsconfig.root.json, work-order.json, .sdlc/flow-graph.json, .sdlc/manifest.json
failure_packet.digest: The qa stage failed and no known error pattern matched. The raw output is below.
failure_packet.decision_reason: an agent reads the failed run's full log and decides what happens next — this script cannot see that log from inside the run that produced it

triage.diagnosis: The QA agent ran to completion and did its job; it just never wrote the one file the workflow gates on. The action returned subtype=success, is_error=false after 323 turns / 51 minutes / $20.19, so the step is green, and the agent left 24 evidence files in qa-evidence/ (a 636-line three-file Playwright suite, 19 screenshots, a HAR, a trace, plus an out-of-band better-sqlite3 check against the Electron registration). check-evidence.mjs then said the report could not be read and the judge's validate rejected it by name — but that is the last step of a long chain, not the break. The break is that nothing in the qa workflow looks at what the agent actually did. The action writes the full transcript to _temp/claude-execution-output.json and the log prints only a metadata line about it; sdlc-qa.yml gives the agent step no id, never runs jq -s -f .sdlc/bin/transcript-summary.jq over that file, and never calls agent-transcript.mjs --recover. sdlc-plan.yml and sdlc-root-cause.yml both do all three, and agent-transcript.mjs was written for exactly this failure (growth-os #20: an agent that reported success and wrote neither expected file). QA is the one agent-emitting stage with no transcript recovery, so this failure mode is structurally invisible here: whether the Write was refused, was aimed at a path outside the upload list, or was simply never made is not answerable from anything this run kept. A prior instance is recorded in the workflow's own comment at sdlc-qa.yml:620-622 ('validate then said the agent did not write qa-report.json and triage answered with another browser session'), and the fix applied then tightened the artifact download — which was a different failure and is why this one recurred undiagnosed. I did not rule out a bad agent run, and I am not claiming one: the evidence shows the suite was built and run and the fix's guard verified working on both platforms, so the QA work is sound. What is missing is not the testing, it is the report and any way to see why it was not written. That is a defect in the pipeline's plumbing, so it escalates rather than re-running: a rerun would burn another ~$20 and ~50 minutes to reach the same dead end, and the next agent would have exactly as much visibility as this one did.
triage.evidence: test job, 'Test it, adversarially': {"type":"result","subtype":"success","is_error":false,"duration_ms":3098783,"num_turns":323,"total_cost_usd":20.19} — success, then 'Did the evidence survive?' logs 'the QA report cannot be read (ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'qa-report.json')', and judge logs 'sdlc: the agent did not write qa-report.json'. Meanwhile upload-artifact reports 'there will be 24 files uploaded' and the qa-evidence artifact (ID 11218775655, 16569296 bytes) downloads intact in judge — so the evidence survived and only the report is missing. The workflow gap: .github/workflows/sdlc-qa.yml has no `id:` on the agent step (so no `steps.<id>.outputs.execution_file`, cf. sdlc-plan.yml:360 and sdlc-root-cause.yml:333), no `jq -s -f .sdlc/bin/transcript-summary.jq` step, and no `agent-transcript.mjs` call (grep for 'transcript' in sdlc-qa.yml returns nothing), while agent-transcript.mjs's own header names this exact failure ('ran 22 turns, reported success, and wrote neither work-order.json nor stop.json ... triage could not tell a Write that was refused from one never made'). Survived work, if a person wants it: PR #11 (OPEN, MERGEABLE, head b635e0f), artifact qa-evidence with qa-evidence/spec/{regexp,regexp-edge}.spec.ts + fixtures.ts, electron-variant-check.txt showing the guard returning 0 for `\`, `#\`, `#[`, `(` and 1 for `#mortgage` on better-sqlite3, and served-tree-probe.txt confirming the preview serves _pr/ at b635e0f with the guard present. Ruled out: transient/outage/limit (a 51-minute agent run completed with is_error=false, no 429/529/timeout, and prior_signatures is empty); a defect in the app's own code (served-tree-probe and electron-variant-check both show the PR's guard installed and semantically correct); a bad work order (work-order.json is intact on the ledger at version 1 and QA's suite maps to its six acceptance criteria).

framework_defect.what: The QA agent step carries no id, no step runs `jq -s -f .sdlc/bin/transcript-summary.jq` over the action's execution file, and no step calls `.sdlc/bin/agent-transcript.mjs --recover qa-report.json` — so when the QA agent finishes without writing qa-report.json, nothing records whether the Write was refused, went to a path outside the upload list, or was never made. sdlc-plan.yml and sdlc-root-cause.yml both wire all three, and agent-transcript.mjs exists for precisely this case; QA is the one artifact-emitting stage with no transcript recovery, which is why run 36983695548 produced only 'the agent did not write qa-report.json' and dispatch-fix classified it error_type=unknown. Its SHAPES map also has no 'qa-report.json' entry, so --recover would need one (keys: verdict, issue, attempt, tests, acceptance_rollup, next_action).
framework_defect.fix: Give the QA agent step an id (e.g. `id: qa_agent`), add a step after it — `if: always()`, env EXEC from `steps.qa_agent.outputs.execution_file` — running `jq -s -f .sdlc/bin/transcript-summary.jq "$EXEC" > qa-transcript.json || true`, add qa-transcript.json to the qa-evidence upload path list, and add a `--recover qa-report.json` invocation of agent-transcript.mjs in the judge job before the validate step; extend SHAPES in .sdlc/bin/agent-transcript.mjs with the qa-report.json key list. That makes a recovered report subject to the same validator and gates as a written one, and prints the tool-call metadata that lets triage tell a refused Write from a missing one.
